structure.title: Forming a practice
structure.text: The first two books give short instructions on conduct, humility, and inward attention. Their subjects recur rather than develop as one proof.

structure.title: Devotion in dialogue
structure.text: Later books turn to inward consolation and communion, often through an exchange between the disciple and Christ.

people.name: The disciple
people.text: The reader the book addresses: a person who wants to follow Christ more closely, and is told to begin by looking honestly at themselves.

people.name: Humility
people.text: The virtue the book returns to again and again: knowing oneself truly, and therefore thinking less of oneself and one's learning.

people.name: Christ
people.text: In the later books Christ speaks directly to the disciple, offering counsel, consolation and correction as a friend would.

context.title: Devotional instruction
context.text: The work assumes Christian belief and aims at a changed practice of life. Its priorities differ from a neutral argument about whether God exists.
context.takeaway: Read each instruction in its devotional setting.

context.title: Learning and vanity
context.text: The criticism of intellectual display concerns what knowledge is used for. Knowing the language of virtue can become a substitute for practising it.
context.takeaway: Watch for the difference between knowing and doing.

notice.text: Notice the wish for praise beneath apparently good actions.
notice.why: The text tests motives as well as results.
Dialogue makes dependence and consolation personal.

opening: It is possible to become learned about humility, speak beautifully about devotion, and still spend the day wanting people to admire you. Thomas à Kempis has little patience for that arrangement. His instructions bring Christianity into the private territory where vanity survives its own exposure: resentment at correction, pleasure in praise, the wish to appear holy. Written for a life of devotion, this book asks for changes that are difficult to display and offers a companionship intended to endure when admiration disappears.
